EKZ Infostealer C2 download and HTTP-POST exfiltration to 83.138.53.110 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts network egress to the FortiBleed/EKZ C2 host 83.138.53.110, including the payload pull at /dl/p.exe and credential exfil POST to /service/save.php. Article-specific because these exact URI paths and the C2 IP are tied to the EKZ Infostealer campaign, not a generic beacon template. Rationale: 83.138.53.110 with URIs /dl/p.exe and /service/save.php is the confirmed EKZ download+exfil endpoint (Arctic Wolf). The two additional IPs are article-listed FortiBleed infrastructure (likely Tor exits — hence lower confidence on those two), so the primary alert weight is on the second-source-confirmed 83.138.53.110. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-via-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/ • https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/fortibleed-attackers-firewalls-credentials-stealers
ATT&CKT1105 T1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel or research hosts intentionally connecting to 83.138.53.110 for sample retrieval
  • Tor exit nodes 185.220.101.15 / 192.42.116.14 being contacted for legitimate Tor usage in the environment
  • Security scanners/crawlers touching the C2 IP during internet-wide scans
  • Sinkhole or takedown infrastructure now resolving to the same IP
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Windows Defender Advanced Threat Protection\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcessFileName driving the connection — powershell.exe or FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe reaching 83.138.53.110 confirms EKZ; check for the /service/save.php POST indicating data left the host. 2) Contain: block 83.138.53.110 at proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and treat any credentials on it (especially browser-stored) as compromised → force password resets. 3) Hunt: pivot on all hosts that resolved/connected to the IP, correlate with FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe execution and C:\ProgramData\log.txt creation to scope the intrusion.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("83.138.53.110","185.220.101.15","192.42.116.14")
    or RemoteUrl has_any ("/dl/p.exe","/service/save.php")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("83.138.53.110","185.220.101.15","192.42.116.14")
    or RequestURL has_any ("/dl/p.exe","/service/save.php")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EKZ Infostealer browser credential theft and staging to C:\ProgramData\log.txt AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts EKZ Infostealer credential collection: a non-browser process touching Chrome 'Local State'/'Login Data' and Firefox key4.db/logins.json/cookies.sqlite, plus creation of the exact exfil staging file C:\ProgramData\log.txt. Article-specific because the staging path and the FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe/PowerShell writer tie directly to the EKZ chain. Rationale: C:\ProgramData\log.txt is the exact EKZ staging file Arctic Wolf documented, and the browser secret stores (Chrome Local State/Login Data, Firefox key4.db/logins.json/cookies.sqlite) are the confirmed harvesting targets. Binding the file writes to the FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe/PowerShell writer keeps this tight to the campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-via-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/05/29/forticlient-ems-vulnerability-infostealer/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate backup/sync software copying browser profile databases (key4.db, Login Data)
  • Browser-migration or password-manager import tools accessing Login Data / logins.json
  • A benign application coincidentally writing C:\ProgramData\log.txt (common generic log filename)
  • Endpoint DLP or forensic collection agents reading browser credential stores
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","OneDrive.exe","Dropbox.exe","backup.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\Application\", @"\Mozilla Firefox\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writer of C:\ProgramData\log.txt is FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe/PowerShell (not a legit app) and check whether browser secret stores were touched in the same session. 2) Contain: isolate host, capture C:\ProgramData\log.txt for scoping, and force-reset all browser-saved and SSO credentials for the user (assume cookies/session tokens stolen → revoke sessions). 3) Hunt: look for the follow-on POST to 83.138.53.110/service/save.php and repeat the file-staging query org-wide across EMS-managed endpoints.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FolderPath =~ @"C:\ProgramData\log.txt" and ActionType == "FileCreated")
    or (FileName in~ ("key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","Login Data","Local State")
        and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe","p.exe","powershell.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFilePath =~ @"C:\ProgramData\log.txt" and EventType == "FileCreated")
    or (TargetFileName in~ ("key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","Login Data","Local State")
        and ActingProcessName has_any ("FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe","p.exe","powershell.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EKZ Infostealer / FortiBleed known-bad file hash execution sweep AIInstallation Medium
Retrospective IOC sweep for execution or on-disk presence of the EKZ Infostealer payload by the exact SHA256/SHA1/MD5 published for the FortiBleed campaign. Article-specific: these are the concrete hashes tied to the fake FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe / p.exe payload. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the published EKZ payload hashes. SHA256 0da123adf9..., SHA1 17e771..., and MD5 338662... are second-source confirmed by Arctic Wolf as the FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe payload; the remaining four SHA256 are article-listed campaign samples included for retro sweep. Hash matches are effectively zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-via-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/forticlient-code-execution-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A malware analyst intentionally detonating the sample in a managed environment
  • Hash collision is not realistic for SHA256 — near-zero false positives
  • EDR quarantine copy of the file being re-scanned and matching the hash
  • Threat-intel enrichment pipeline re-hashing a stored artifact
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the match host and whether it was process execution (active infection) vs. a dormant file drop; capture full path and initiating command line. 2) Contain: isolate host, block all listed hashes in EDR, and quarantine the artifact; assume EKZ ran → treat local credentials as compromised. 3) Hunt: expand to the process-tree, C2 (83.138.53.110), and staging-file detections; check the FortiClient EMS server for CVE-2026-35616 exploitation as the entry point.
let Sha256 = dynamic(["0da123adf9251957a4b850a3f6bd6a753dd4892be176a84a18450e899534cc5e","d91c00fad521e76efa89715cca89db487d5676f2c767c883482f9c8f82bd383a","fd65051c61a904a304919c04a8c8633c001183ac73ac461cd4d9057946f02bf5","2927bc31b4f8254c6b332fc03110a6373cad00ffa2ff9de427c26bb222017bb2","2f25ea1b622abf3212141af932c2ec4cbd6b2b5903c2a531121f691227d98cff"]);
union
  (DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where SHA256 in~ (Sha256) or SHA1 =~ "17e771c78430cc67e71d4547f8996a1a488e9d3f" or MD5 =~ "338662fd0c4d750a0ba203a32b59f081"
    | extend Evt="ProcessCreated", Cmd=ProcessCommandLine),
  (DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where SHA256 in~ (Sha256) or SHA1 =~ "17e771c78430cc67e71d4547f8996a1a488e9d3f" or MD5 =~ "338662fd0c4d750a0ba203a32b59f081"
    | extend Evt=ActionType, Cmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Evt, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, SHA1, MD5, Cmd
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in~ ("0da123adf9251957a4b850a3f6bd6a753dd4892be176a84a18450e899534cc5e","d91c00fad521e76efa89715cca89db487d5676f2c767c883482f9c8f82bd383a","fd65051c61a904a304919c04a8c8633c001183ac73ac461cd4d9057946f02bf5","2927bc31b4f8254c6b332fc03110a6373cad00ffa2ff9de427c26bb222017bb2","2f25ea1b622abf3212141af932c2ec4cbd6b2b5903c2a531121f691227d98cff")

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35616")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35616")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer

status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/

            - '\mshta.exe'

            - 'invoke-expression'

            - 'downloadstring'

        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["0da123adf9251957a4b850a3f6bd6a753dd4892be176a84a18450e899534cc5e", "d91c00fad521e76efa89715cca89db487d5676f2c767c883482f9c8f82bd383a", "fd65051c61a904a304919c04a8c8633c001183ac73ac461cd4d9057946f02bf5", "2927bc31b4f8254c6b332fc03110a6373cad00ffa2ff9de427c26bb222017bb2", "2f25ea1b622abf3212141af932c2ec4cbd6b2b5903c2a531121f691227d98cff", "17e771c78430cc67e71d4547f8996a1a488e9d3f", "338662fd0c4d750a0ba203a32b59f081"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New ChocoPoC RAT Targets Vulnerability Researchers via Fake PoC Exploit Repos

The Hacker News
2026-07-02 15 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Attackers are hiding a data-stealing trojan inside fake exploit code aimed at the people who hunt bugs for a living. The malware, called ChocoPoC, travels in Python proof-of-concept (PoC) repositories on GitHub that claim to exploit hot new CVEs. Run one, and it quietly lifts your saved passwords, browser cookies, and files, then hands the attacker a shell on your machine.&nbsp;YesWeHack and

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] PoC script executed from clone/Downloads/Temp within 2 min of git clone · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — New ChocoPoC RAT Targets Vulnerability Researchers via Fake PoC Exploit Repos
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Install of ChocoPoC malicious PyPI packages (frint/skytext/slogsec/logcrypt.cryptography) · [LLM] ChocoPoC gradient native loader written/loaded (gradient.pyd / gradient.so) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Python beaconing to Mapbox dead-drop / DoH resolvers (ChocoPoC C2) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Outbound connection to ChocoPoC exfiltration server 91.132.163.78 · [LLM] Python process reading browser credential stores and SSH/cloud secrets · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Install of ChocoPoC malicious PyPI packages (frint/skytext/slogsec/logcrypt.cryptography) AIInstallation High
Hunts pip installation of the exact malicious dependency packages ChocoPoC ships in fake PoC repos. These package names are the highest-fidelity IOC in the campaign because they exist only to sideload the RAT loader. Rationale: Package names frint/skytext/slogsec/logcrypt.cryptography are named directly in the article and corroborated by BleepingComputer and CyberSecurityNews; they have no legitimate use, so a pip-install match is effectively a true positive. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-chocopoc-malware-targets-researchers-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-mapbox-dead-drop-c2/ • https://cyberpress.org/chocopoc-targets-python-dependencies/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign internal package legitimately named similarly to 'skytext' or 'logcrypt' hosted on a private index
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating the sample in a sandbox for analysis
  • Threat-intel automation pulling the IOC package to reproduce the report
  • A typo'd but harmless install attempt of an unrelated package containing the substring 'frint'
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--index-url","--extra-index-url") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "internal")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full pip command line and the host owner; confirm the target package is the campaign IOC and not an internal lookalike on a private index. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill python/pip, and treat all local browser, SSH and cloud credentials on that host as compromised — rotate them. 3) Hunt: search the same host for gradient.pyd/gradient.so writes, outbound to 91.132.163.78, and python-driven access to browser credential stores (UC5).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","pip","pip3","python.exe","python3","python")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "install"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("frint","skytext","slogsec","logcrypt.cryptography","logcrypt")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("pip","python") or ParentProcessName has_any ("pip","python")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "install"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("frint","skytext","slogsec","logcrypt.cryptography","logcrypt")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ChocoPoC Malicious PyPI Package Install (frint/skytext/slogsec/logcrypt)
id: 6b1c9e2a-2f74-4a1d-9e3b-7c0f8a1d54aa
description: Detects pip installation of the ChocoPoC campaign's malicious dependency packages that sideload a Python RAT into fake PoC exploit repos.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-chocopoc-rat-targets-vulnerability.html
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-chocopoc-malware-targets-researchers-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1195.001
  - attack.t1059.006
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_tool:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\pip.exe'
      - '\pip3.exe'
      - '\python.exe'
      - '/pip'
      - '/pip3'
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
  selection_install:
    CommandLine|contains: 'install'
  selection_pkg:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'frint'
      - 'skytext'
      - 'slogsec'
      - 'logcrypt.cryptography'
  condition: selection_tool and selection_install and selection_pkg
level: high
(source:linux.auditd OR source:windows.sysmon) (@process.command_line:(*install*) OR @CommandLine:(*install*)) (@process.command_line:(*frint* OR *skytext* OR *slogsec* OR *logcrypt*) OR @CommandLine:(*frint* OR *skytext* OR *slogsec* OR *logcrypt*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/(pip3?|python3?)(\.exe)?$/i
| CommandLine=/install/i
| CommandLine=/(frint|skytext|slogsec|logcrypt)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","pip","pip3","python.exe","python3","python")) (Processes.process="*install*") (Processes.process="*frint*" OR Processes.process="*skytext*" OR Processes.process="*slogsec*" OR Processes.process="*logcrypt.cryptography*" OR Processes.process="*logcrypt*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","pip","pip3","python.exe","python3","python")) (Processes.process="*install*") (Processes.process="*frint*" OR Processes.process="*skytext*" OR Processes.process="*slogsec*" OR Processes.process="*logcrypt.cryptography*" OR Processes.process="*logcrypt*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
ChocoPoC gradient native loader written/loaded (gradient.pyd / gradient.so) AIInstallation High
Hunts creation or module-load of the skytext compiled extension gradient.pyd (Windows) or gradient.so (Linux) that executes the moment a PoC is launched. This is the on-disk artifact that unpacks and downloads the RAT. Rationale: gradient.pyd/gradient.so are the exact compiled-loader filenames named in the article and confirmed by Cyberpress; a native Python extension called 'gradient' shipped by an untrusted package is not a normal artifact. Cross-checked against: • https://cyberpress.org/chocopoc-targets-python-dependencies/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-chocopoc-malware-targets-researchers-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/
ATT&CKT1129 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An unrelated legitimate ML/plotting library that ships a native module coincidentally named gradient.so
  • Sandbox detonation of the sample by an analyst
  • Developer building a local C-extension named gradient for testing
  • Container image build layer that includes a benign gradient extension
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3","python") or ActingProcessName has "python"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the file hash and the parent process; confirm the loading process is python and the path is under a cloned repo / site-packages of skytext. 2) Contain: isolate host, quarantine gradient.pyd/gradient.so, block outbound to 91.132.163.78. 3) Hunt: pivot on the SHA256 across the fleet and check DeviceProcessEvents for the preceding skytext/frint install (UC1) and subsequent credential access (UC5).
union
( DeviceImageLoadEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName in~ ("gradient.pyd","gradient.so")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Action="ImageLoad", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256 ),
( DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName in~ ("gradient.pyd","gradient.so")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Action="FileWrite", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256 )
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("gradient.pyd","gradient.so")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ChocoPoC gradient Native Loader File Event
id: 9d2e4f11-7a63-4b98-8c21-0f6b3d7e2c55
description: Detects the skytext compiled Python extension gradient.pyd/gradient.so being written or loaded, the ChocoPoC in-repo trigger that downloads the RAT.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-chocopoc-rat-targets-vulnerability.html
  - https://cyberpress.org/chocopoc-targets-python-dependencies/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:

  - attack.t1129
  - attack.t1204.002
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\gradient.pyd'
      - '/gradient.so'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\gradient.pyd OR *\\Gradient.pyd OR *\\GRADIENT.PYD) OR (source:linux.auditd @TargetFilename:(*/gradient.so))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/gradient\.(pyd|so)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN ("gradient.pyd","gradient.so")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN ("gradient.pyd","gradient.so")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
PoC script executed from clone/Downloads/Temp within 2 min of git clone AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the ChocoPoC infection habit: a researcher clones a fake PoC repo then runs python/powershell against EXPLOIT_POC.py (or poc/exploit .py) from a Downloads, Temp or /tmp clone path seconds later — the moment the compiled loader triggers. Rationale: Anchors on the article's EXPLOIT_POC.py trigger-file name plus the clone-and-run researcher behavior described as the infection route; the git-clone→python within 120s window strips generic PoC testing noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-chocopoc-malware-targets-researchers-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-mapbox-dead-drop-c2/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1204.001 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate red-teamer safely running a clean community PoC in a lab VM
  • CI pipeline that clones a repo and runs its poc.py test harness
  • Researcher re-running a previously vetted exploit.py from Downloads
  • Automated malware-analysis harness detonating PoCs by design
Suppression filter
| where CloneCmd has_any ("github.com","gitlab.com") and DelaySec <= 120
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the CloneCmd URL — is the source repo a brand-new/unknown GitHub account tied to a hot CVE? Check whether skytext/frint were installed on the host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, snapshot for forensics, and rotate any credentials that lived on it. 3) Hunt: check the host for gradient.pyd/.so (UC2), outbound to 91.132.163.78 (UC4), and Mapbox/DoH beaconing by python (UC6).
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let WindowSec = 120;
let GitClones = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where FileName in~ ("git.exe","git") and ProcessCommandLine has "clone"
    | project GitTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, CloneCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where FileName in~ ("python.exe","python3","python","powershell.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("EXPLOIT_POC","exploit.py","poc.py")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/Downloads/")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| join kind=inner GitClones on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (GitTime .. GitTime + WindowSec*1s)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, CloneCmd, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, GitTime)
| order by Timestamp desc
let Window = 120s;
let GitClones = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ActingProcessName has "git" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "clone"
    | project GitTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, CloneCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","powershell")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("EXPLOIT_POC","exploit.py","poc.py")
| join kind=inner GitClones on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (GitTime .. GitTime + Window)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, CloneCmd, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, GitTime)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
(source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:(*EXPLOIT_POC* OR *exploit.py* OR *poc.py*) @process.command_line:(*python* OR */tmp/* OR *Downloads*)) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\python.exe OR *\\Python.exe OR *\\powershell.exe) @CommandLine:(*EXPLOIT_POC* OR *exploit.py* OR *poc.py*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/(python3?|powershell)(\.exe)?$/i
| CommandLine=/(EXPLOIT_POC|exploit\.py|poc\.py)/i
| CommandLine=/(Downloads|Temp|\/tmp\/)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("python.exe","python3","python","powershell.exe")) (Processes.process IN ("*EXPLOIT_POC*","*exploit.py*","*poc.py*")) (Processes.process_path IN ("*\\Downloads\\*","*\\Temp\\*","*/tmp/*","*/Downloads/*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("python.exe","python3","python","powershell.exe")) (Processes.process IN ("*EXPLOIT_POC*","*exploit.py*","*poc.py*")) (Processes.process_path IN ("*\\Downloads\\*","*\\Temp\\*","*/tmp/*","*/Downloads/*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Outbound connection to ChocoPoC exfiltration server 91.132.163.78 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts any host connecting to the ChocoPoC large-upload/exfiltration server 91.132.163.78. This is the out-of-band channel the RAT uses for bulk file/folder uploads, separate from its Mapbox dead-drop control channel. Rationale: 91.132.163.78 is the single hard IOC IP named in the article for large uploads and is confirmed still-live by CyberSecurityNews; a static IP match has near-zero ambiguity. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-mapbox-dead-drop-c2/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-chocopoc-malware-targets-researchers-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel sandbox intentionally connecting to the IOC to validate it is live
  • A researcher's automated IOC-reachability sweep
  • Coincidental reuse of the same hosting IP by an unrelated benign service after takedown
  • Security scanner reaching the IP as part of an internet-wide scan
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — python/gradient indicates confirmed ChocoPoC exfil; note bytes_out to gauge data loss. 2) Contain: block 91.132.163.78 at egress, isolate the host, and preserve netflow/pcap. 3) Hunt: on the same host confirm skytext/frint install (UC1), gradient loader (UC2), and browser/SSH credential access (UC5); assume any credentials/reports on the host are exfiltrated and rotate.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "91.132.163.78"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "91.132.163.78"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, NetworkBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Python process reading browser credential stores and SSH/cloud secrets AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the ChocoPoC stealer behavior: a python-hosted process reading Chrome/Brave/Edge/Firefox login/cookie databases plus ~/.ssh and ~/.aws secrets. Ties the RAT's credential harvesting to its Python execution context. Rationale: Article states ChocoPoC pulls saved passwords/cookies/history from Chrome, Brave, Edge and Firefox and grabs local databases and shell/network config; scoping the browser secret-store and ~/.ssh|~/.aws reads to a python initiator ties the theft to the RAT's Python runtime. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-chocopoc-malware-targets-researchers-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/ • https://cyberpress.org/chocopoc-targets-python-dependencies/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1552.001 T1539
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate python browser-automation (Selenium profile handling) touching Login Data
  • A credential-harvesting security tool the researcher runs on purpose (e.g. a browser-cred audit script)
  • Backup software written in python snapshotting the user profile
  • Python dotfile/SSH management tooling reading ~/.ssh/config
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("selenium","playwright") or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("selenium","playwright"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the python command line and parent — is it tied to a freshly cloned PoC or skytext/gradient? Legit automation usually runs from a known project path. 2) Contain: isolate the host and immediately rotate browser-saved passwords, session cookies, SSH keys and cloud (AWS) credentials for that user. 3) Hunt: correlate with outbound to 91.132.163.78 (UC4) and Mapbox/DoH beaconing (UC6) to confirm exfiltration; expand credential rotation to any client/engagement secrets stored on the host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3","python")
| where (FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","Web Data","id_rsa","credentials"))
    or (FolderPath has_any ("/.ssh/","/.aws/",@"\.ssh\",@"\.aws\"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "python"
| where (TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","Web Data","id_rsa","credentials"))
    or (TargetFilePath has_any ("/.ssh/","/.aws/",@"\.ssh\",@"\.aws\"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: c71e0a95-4d38-4d0a-8b6e-2a1f9c6e3b40
description: Detects a python-hosted process accessing browser login/cookie databases or ~/.ssh and ~/.aws secrets, matching ChocoPoC credential theft.
references:

logsource:

Python beaconing to Mapbox dead-drop / DoH resolvers (ChocoPoC C2) AICommand & Control Low
Hunts ChocoPoC's covert control channel: a python-hosted process resolving/contacting Mapbox and DNS-over-HTTPS resolver endpoints, which the RAT abuses as a domain-fronted dead drop for its orders. Rationale: Article specifies the RAT reads orders from a Mapbox dataset used as a dead drop, resolving it over DNS-over-HTTPS with a domain-fronting trick; scoping Mapbox/DoH-resolver contact to a python initiator surfaces that channel while excluding normal browser Mapbox usage. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-mapbox-dead-drop-c2/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-chocopoc-malware-targets-researchers-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/
ATT&CKT1102 T1090.004 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A python GIS/mapping app legitimately calling the Mapbox API
  • A python tool configured to use DoH (cloudflare-dns.com / dns.google) for privacy
  • Data-science notebooks fetching Mapbox tiles
  • Corporate DoH-based DNS client written in python
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("geopandas","folium","mapbox","rasterio"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating python has no legitimate mapping/GIS purpose and correlate timing with a recent PoC clone or skytext install. 2) Contain: isolate the host; block the offending Mapbox dataset/DoH endpoint at egress if not business-required. 3) Hunt: pivot to bulk uploads to 91.132.163.78 (UC4) and credential store access (UC5); pull the Mapbox account/dataset id from proxy logs for takedown reporting. Sentinel note: DoH/Mapbox is high-FP without process context (ImDnsActivity lacks initiator), so treat as a fleet-wide hunt not an alert.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3","python")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.mapbox.com","mapbox.com","cloudflare-dns.com","dns.google","mozilla.cloudflare-dns.com","doh.opendns.com")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("api.mapbox.com","mapbox.com","cloudflare-dns.com","dns.google","doh.opendns.com")
| summarize QueryCount = count(), Queries = make_set(DnsQuery, 20) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\python.exe OR *\\Python.exe) @DestinationHostname:(*mapbox.com* OR *cloudflare-dns.com* OR *dns.google* OR *doh.opendns.com*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| ContextImageFileName=/(python3?)(\.exe)?$/i
| DomainName=/(mapbox\.com|cloudflare-dns\.com|dns\.google|doh\.opendns\.com)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query IN ("*api.mapbox.com*","*mapbox.com*","*cloudflare-dns.com*","*dns.google*","*doh.opendns.com*")) by DNS.src DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query IN ("*api.mapbox.com*","*mapbox.com*","*cloudflare-dns.com*","*dns.google*","*doh.opendns.com*")) by DNS.src DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1555.003

logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

SharePoint RCE CVE-2026-45659 Added to CISA KEV After Active Exploitation

The Hacker News
2026-07-02 15 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Wednesday added a high-severity flaw impacting Microsoft SharePoint Server to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-45659 (CVSS score: 8.8), is a case of remote code execution arising from the deserialization of untrusted data. The issue

SharePoint/Triofox LFI probing for win.ini & web.config (Storm-2603 initial access) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to internet-facing SharePoint/Gladinet Triofox endpoints that retrieve win.ini or web.config (including the corroborated /storage/t.dn LFI endpoint used to steal the ASP.NET machineKey). This is the article's stated initial-access probe preceding CVE-2025-11371 / CVE-2026-45659 exploitation. Rationale: Uses the article's exact LFI artifacts (win.ini, web.config) plus the second-source Huntress-confirmed /storage/t.dn and UploadDownloadProxy Triofox endpoints; retrieval of web.config yields the machineKey enabling ViewState RCE, so a served (status<400) hit is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/gladinet-centrestack-triofox-local-file-inclusion-flaw • https://thehackernews.com/2025/10/from-lfi-to-rce-active-exploitation.html • https://securityaffairs.com/183259/hacking/cve-2025-11371-unpatched-zero-day-in-gladinet-centrestack-triofox-under-attack.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) probing for LFI as part of authorized assessments
  • Legitimate SharePoint health-check tooling reading web.config over HTTP
  • Backup/config-management agents fetching web.config via web endpoints
  • Security researchers or red-team engagements hitting /storage/t.dn
Suppression filter
| where csUserAgent !has_any ("Nessus", "Qualys", "nmap", "masscan", "Nuclei") and cIP !in ("10.0.0.0/8")   // exclude sanctioned scanners / internal ranges
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the source IP and confirm whether web.config/machineKey content was actually returned (status 200 + response size); check if the source IP is an internal scanner or external. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/perimeter and, if a served web.config is confirmed, rotate the SharePoint/Triofox ASP.NET machineKey and force IIS recycle to invalidate forged ViewState. 3) Hunt: on the affected server look for follow-on ViewState deserialization POSTs, w3wp.exe spawning cmd/powershell, and any Velociraptor or remote-access-tool execution within the following hours.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csMethod == "GET"
| where csUriStem has_any ("win.ini", "web.config", "t.dn") or csUriQuery has_any ("win.ini", "web.config")
| where scStatus < 400   // only successful/served retrievals of the sensitive file
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent, sSiteName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Velociraptor DFIR agent executed as attacker tooling (Storm-2603 execution) AIInstallation High
Hunts execution or service install of the Velociraptor DFIR binary on hosts that are not sanctioned incident-response endpoints. The article states Storm-2603 deployed Velociraptor with SYSTEM privileges to blend malicious activity with trusted admin behaviour. Rationale: Velociraptor is named explicitly in the article as the DFIR tool Storm-2603 abused; the binary name, client artifact strings, and SYSTEM-integrity execution are distinctive and rare outside sanctioned IR, giving low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/velociraptor-misuse-part-two-eye-of-the-storm • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/velociraptor-incident-response-tool-abused-for-remote-access • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-velociraptor-cloudflare-tunnels-zoho-assist/
ATT&CKT1105 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Your own DFIR/IR team legitimately deploying Velociraptor during an investigation
  • MSSP or Sophos/Huntress-managed Velociraptor agent as a sanctioned monitoring tool
  • Security lab / detection-engineering testing of Velociraptor
  • Threat-hunting exercises running the binary on a jump-host
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("IR-JUMPHOST01", "DFIR-TOOLS01")   // populate with sanctioned IR endpoints
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host is a sanctioned IR endpoint and whether your team deployed Velociraptor; inspect the config/frontend URL in the command line to see where it reports (attacker C2 vs internal). 2) Contain: if unauthorized, isolate the host, kill the Velociraptor process/service, and capture the config file for the C2 address. 3) Hunt: pivot on the config's frontend domain across DeviceNetworkEvents, and look for co-occurring new admin accounts, cloudflared tunnels, and NSecKrnl.sys driver drops on the same and adjacent hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "velociraptor.exe"
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("velociraptor", "artifact_collector", "Velociraptor.Client", "--config", "frontend")
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Velociraptor"
// exclude sanctioned DFIR jump-hosts by DeviceName if you have them
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessIntegrityLevel, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| sort by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\velociraptor.exe" or CommandLine has_any ("velociraptor", "artifact_collector", "Velociraptor.Client")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

NSecKrnl.sys vulnerable driver drop/install (Storm-2603 BYOVD EDR tampering) AIInstallation High
Hunts creation on disk or service installation of the vulnerable NSecKrnl.sys driver, which the article states was used as a BYOVD conduit to tamper with endpoint protection and reduce visibility. Any appearance of this driver name is high-signal. Rationale: NSecKrnl.sys is the exact vulnerable driver named in the article as the BYOVD conduit for EDR tampering; a fixed, uncommon driver filename makes any hit essentially a true positive. Cross-checked against: • https://cyberpress.org/multiple-attackers-one-network/ • https://gbhackers.com/microsoft-uncovers-parallel-threat-activity/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4188359/unpatched-sharepoint-servers-opened-the-door-to-multiple-attackers-microsoft-finds.html
ATT&CKT1068 T1562.001 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate product that genuinely ships a driver literally named NSecKrnl.sys (verify vendor signature and path)
  • Security-research/malware-analysis sandbox intentionally detonating the BYOVD sample
  • Restore of a forensic image that contains the artifact
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path, SHA256 and signer of NSecKrnl.sys and the process that wrote it (InitiatingProcessFileName); check whether a matching kernel service was registered (7045). 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately, block the driver hash org-wide, and treat EDR telemetry from that host as untrusted (assume tampering) — validate the sensor is still reporting. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints for the same driver hash/name and service, and correlate with Velociraptor execution, new admin accounts, and EDR sensor-stop/config-change events around the same timestamp.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "NSecKrnl.sys"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| sort by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (7045, 4697)
| where ServiceFileName has "NSecKrnl" or ServiceName has "NSecKrnl"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType, ServiceAccount
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Attacker remote-access channels: cloudflared tunnel, Zoho Assist, VS Code SSH tunnel AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts execution of the three specific redundant remote-access channels the article attributes to Storm-2603 for persistent C2: Cloudflare tunneling (cloudflared tunnel), Zoho Assist agents, and Visual Studio Code SSH/remote tunnels. Targets server assets where these tools are not normally present. Rationale: The three channels (Cloudflare tunneling, Zoho Assist, VS Code SSH) are named verbatim in the article and confirmed by second sources; scoping cloudflared/code to the 'tunnel' subcommand keeps the signal on the actual tunnel behaviour rather than benign launches. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-velociraptor-cloudflare-tunnels-zoho-assist/ • https://cyberpress.org/multiple-attackers-one-network/ • https://gbhackers.com/microsoft-uncovers-parallel-threat-activity/
ATT&CKT1572 T1219 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers legitimately running 'code tunnel' (VS Code Remote Tunnels) on workstations
  • IT support using Zoho Assist as a sanctioned remote-support tool
  • Sanctioned Cloudflare Tunnel deployment for internal app publishing
  • CI/CD or dev machines with cloudflared for local testing
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "DEV" and DeviceName !has "WKS"   // reduce developer-workstation noise; keep server/DC assets in scope
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the host is a server/DC (high suspicion) vs a developer workstation, and inspect the tunnel target — cloudflared config/token, Zoho session ID, or VS Code tunnel name — for external ownership. 2) Contain: on server/infrastructure assets, kill the process and any associated service, and block the tunnel egress domains (*.trycloudflare.com, *.cloudflare.com tunnels, zoho assist domains) from that host. 3) Hunt: correlate the same host/account with Velociraptor, NSecKrnl.sys, and new admin-account creation, and check whether the same remote-access tooling appears on a second organization/host (article notes lateral movement into a second org).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "cloudflared.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "tunnel")
    or FileName in~ ("ZA_Access.exe", "ZA_Connect.exe", "ZMAgent.exe", "ZohoMeeting.exe", "ZohoURS.exe")
    or (FileName =~ "code.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "tunnel")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| sort by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\cloudflared.exe" and CommandLine has "tunnel")
    or NewProcessName has_any ("ZA_Access.exe", "ZA_Connect.exe", "ZMAgent.exe", "ZohoMeeting.exe", "ZohoURS.exe")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\code.exe" and CommandLine has "tunnel")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

New local/domain admin account creation and privileged-group grant (Storm-2603 persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts creation of new accounts followed by (or directly) their addition to Administrators / Domain Admins / Enterprise Admins, and command-line net user/group /add of admin members. The article states Storm-2603 escalated by creating new local and domain administrator accounts. Rationale: Directly targets the article's 'created new local and domain administrator accounts' behaviour via both auth telemetry (4728/4732 to well-known admin SID S-1-5-32-544) and the net.exe /add command line, which is the concrete on-host method. Cross-checked against: • https://cyberpress.org/multiple-attackers-one-network/ • https://gbhackers.com/microsoft-uncovers-parallel-threat-activity/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4188359/unpatched-sharepoint-servers-opened-the-door-to-multiple-attackers-microsoft-finds.html
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1136.002 T1078.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned IT provisioning of new admin accounts during onboarding/imaging
  • Identity-management/PAM automation adding accounts to privileged groups
  • Legitimate helpdesk scripts using net localgroup administrators /add
  • Domain migration or M&A activity creating admin accounts in bulk
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-idm", "svc-provisioning") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("pam_agent.exe")   // exclude sanctioned provisioning identities
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the actor (SubjectUserName/InitiatingProcessAccountName) and the created account; confirm whether a change ticket exists and whether the actor is itself a recently-created or compromised account. 2) Contain: disable the newly created account, remove it from privileged groups, and force a password reset on the actor account; on a DC, verify replication of the malicious group change is reversed. 3) Hunt: correlate the new account's first logons across hosts (lateral movement to a second org per the article), and check for co-occurring Velociraptor, cloudflared/Zoho/VS Code tunnels, and NSecKrnl.sys on the same hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("net.exe", "net1.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/add"
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "user") or (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("localgroup", "group") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("administrators", "domain admins", "enterprise admins"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| sort by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (4728, 4732)   // member added to global (4728) / local (4732) security-enabled group
| where TargetSid == "S-1-5-32-544" or TargetUserName in~ ("Administrators", "Domain Admins", "Enterprise Admins")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Actor = SubjectUserName, AddedMember = MemberName, Group = TargetUserName, EventID
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
title: New Admin Account via net.exe user/group add

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45659", "CVE-2025-11371")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45659", "CVE-2025-11371")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
