Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Ghost cache-poisoning via unauthenticated x-ghost-preview header (CVE-2026-53943)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Ghost cache-poisoning via unauthenticated x-ghost-preview header (CVE-2026-53943) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests carrying the `x-ghost-preview` header hitting a Ghost frontend behind a shared cache (Fastly/Cloudflare/nginx proxy_cache). An unauthenticated attacker uses this header to alter the rendered response, which the shared cache then stores and serves to other visitors — enabling reflected/stored XSS and, on same-domain admin deployments, staff-account takeover. Rationale: The `x-ghost-preview` request header is the exact, article-named injection vector for CVE-2026-53943 and is not a benign header any normal browser or bot emits — its presence in inbound edge/WAF logs is a near-zero-FP signal. Splunk uses TERM() to match the header token in raw web events (headers are not first-class CIM Web fields); Sentinel searches the CEF Message/RequestContext where WAFs surface matched request headers. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-62q6-4hv4-vjrw • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-53943
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ghost's own preview/staging workflow where an authenticated editor legitimately requests preview content (the header is used as designed) — distinguishable by an accompanying valid admin session cookie/authenticated source IP
  • Security-scanning tools (Burp, Nuclei, internal DAST) firing the CVE-2026-53943 test payload during an authorized assessment
  • Synthetic-monitoring or QA scripts that replay saved requests including custom headers
  • A misconfigured internal proxy that unconditionally forwards/injects a preview header on all upstream requests
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestClientApplication has_any ("Burp","Nuclei","HealthCheck","pingdom","StatusCake") or SourceIP in ("127.0.0.1"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the target host runs Ghost <= v6.36.0 and whether frontend and admin share the same domain (same-domain = staff-takeover exposure). Check whether the shared cache stored the response (look for a subsequent cache-HIT on the same URL/varied output) and identify the source IP + user-agent. 2) CONTAIN: At the caching layer, add a rule to bypass/deny cache for any request bearing `x-ghost-preview`; purge the affected cache keys/URLs. Upgrade Ghost to v6.37.0+. If same-domain admin and poisoning is confirmed, use Settings > Danger Zone > 'Reset all authentication' (Ghost v6.41.0+) to invalidate staff sessions. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the source IP for other header-injection or preview-abuse attempts; review admin/staff sign-ins and session activity after the poisoning window for signs of account takeover; check edge logs for other cached poisoned URLs served to third parties.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor in~ ("Fastly","Cloudflare","NGINX","Imperva","F5","Akamai") or DeviceProduct has_any ("WAF","proxy","cache")
| where Message has "x-ghost-preview" or RequestContext has "x-ghost-preview"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fleet valuesFrom cross-namespace secret/configmap reference (CVE-2026-44935) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts Rancher Fleet GitRepo/HelmOp/Bundle custom resources whose spec contains a `valuesFrom` block with a secretKeyRef/configMapKeyRef, the exact mechanism CVE-2026-44935 abuses to read secrets in namespaces the tenant is not authorized for. Article-specific because it pivots on the Fleet CRD resource names plus the `valuesFrom` key-reference structure rather than generic secret access. Rationale: Uses the exact Fleet CRD resource names (gitrepos/helmops/bundles from go:github.com/rancher/fleet) and the `valuesFrom` + secretKeyRef/configMapKeyRef structure named in GHSA-xr65-5cpm-g36x as the exploitation vector; high-fidelity because legitimate fleet.yaml normally references secrets in the same namespace only. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xr65-5cpm-g36x • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/007/
ATT&CKT1552.007
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate multi-namespace GitOps deployment where an operator intentionally references a shared config namespace
  • Fleet platform team testing valuesFrom against a sanctioned central secrets namespace
  • CI pipelines that template Bundles with valuesFrom to a common values ConfigMap
  • Upgrade migrations that recreate existing GitRepo resources with unchanged valuesFrom blocks
Suppression filter
| where not (Username has "system:serviceaccount:cattle-fleet-system" and ObjNamespace == extract(@"namespace:\s*([a-z0-9-]+)", 1, ReqStr))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full RequestObject; compare the namespace inside valuesFrom to ObjectRef.namespace and to the tenant that owns the requesting Username — a mismatch to a namespace the tenant has no RBAC in is the true positive. 2) Contain: delete/suspend the offending GitRepo/HelmOp/Bundle, and rotate any secret whose name/namespace/key appears in the valuesFrom reference (advisory explicitly recommends rotation). 3) Hunt: enumerate all Fleet CRs created by the same Username across the cluster and check whether the Fleet agent service account subsequently read those referenced secrets (see companion fan-out UC).
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| extend ObjResource = tostring(ObjectRef.resource), ObjNamespace = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace)
| where ObjResource in ("gitrepos","helmops","bundles")
| extend ReqStr = tostring(RequestObject)
| where ReqStr has "valuesFrom" and (ReqStr has "secretKeyRef" or ReqStr has "configMapKeyRef")
| where ReqStr has "namespace"    // cross-namespace ref requires an explicit namespace inside valuesFrom
| project TimeGenerated, Username, Verb, ObjResource, ObjNamespace, RequestUri, ReqStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fleet agent service account reads secrets across multiple namespaces (CVE-2026-44935) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the downstream-cluster fingerprint of CVE-2026-44935: the Fleet agent service account issuing get/list of secrets or configmaps across an abnormal number of distinct namespaces within a short window, indicating cross-tenant credential harvesting via unrestricted valuesFrom/HelmOp deployment. Article-specific because it keys on the Fleet agent SA identity and the cross-namespace fan-out the advisory tells defenders to review logs for. Rationale: Pivots on the Fleet agent service account identity (cattle-fleet-system fleet-agent) reading secrets/configmaps across namespaces — the exact post-exploit behaviour GHSA-xr65-5cpm-g36x tells operators to review cluster logs for and to drive credential rotation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xr65-5cpm-g36x • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/007/
ATT&CKT1552.007 T1613
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate multi-tenant cluster where the Fleet agent SA is authorized to deploy into many namespaces by design
  • Initial Fleet onboarding/bootstrap that syncs bundles into a large set of namespaces at once
  • Backup/DR tooling running under a fleet-labelled SA enumerating secrets
  • Cluster-wide chart rollout (e.g. cert-manager, monitoring) driven through Fleet touching every namespace
Response runbook
1) Triage: list the distinct namespaces and secret names the Fleet agent SA touched; confirm against the tenant boundary — reads into namespaces owned by a different tenant are the true positive. 2) Contain: rotate the Fleet agent service account token and every secret it read cross-tenant, then apply the patched-version Policy resource pinning a least-privilege service account per GitRepo/HelmOp/Bundle namespace. 3) Hunt: correlate back to companion UC (valuesFrom cross-namespace references) to identify which GitRepo/HelmOp/Bundle CR triggered the reads and which tenant Username authored it; upgrade Fleet to v0.15.2/v0.14.6/0.13.11/v0.12.15.

| where NamespaceCount > 3    // 3 = a single Fleet agent normally serves a bounded tenant namespace set; fan-out beyond that is the CVE signal
| order by NamespaceCount desc

Rancher /v3/import authImage YAML injection via URL-encoded newlines (CVE-2026-44939) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound web requests to the Rancher cluster-import endpoint /v3/import/{token}_{clusterId}.yaml where the authImage query parameter carries URL-encoded newlines (%0A/%0D) or raw newlines — the exact YAML-breakout primitive used to inject arbitrary manifest keys. Article-specific because it keys on the concrete endpoint path plus the authImage parameter plus the newline breakout characters, not a generic web attack. Rationale: Uses the exact article strings: endpoint '/v3/import/', parameter 'authImage', and the URL-encoded newline breakout (%0A/%0D) named as the patch target. Legitimate agent-image overrides never contain newline encodings, so FP rate is very low. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-44939 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/rancher/rancher/CVE-2026-44939/ • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2026-44939
ATT&CKT1190 T1610
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners (Nessus/Nuclei) probing the /v3/import endpoint with crafted payloads during authorized pentests
  • Rancher agent troubleshooting where an operator manually URL-encodes an image tag containing a '+' or ':' (rare, and won't include %0A/%0D)
  • WAF/proxy that double-decodes and re-logs the query string, producing a benign echoed value
  • Automated CI that templates import URLs and accidentally embeds a trailing whitespace character
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nessus","nuclei","Nuclei","masscan")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full RequestURL and URL-decode the authImage value; confirm it contains newline bytes followed by injected YAML keys (command:, hostPath, hostNetwork). Note SourceIP and whether the request returned 200. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the WAF, invalidate/rotate the affected cluster registration token, and confirm Rancher is on a patched build (>= 2.14.2/2.13.6/2.12.10/2.11.14/2.10.12). 3) Hunt: pivot to Kubernetes audit logs for any DaemonSet create/update in cattle-system named kube-api-auth carrying command:/args:, and search endpoints for kubectl apply of the same import URL.
CommonSecurityLog

| where RequestURL has "/v3/import/"

| where RequestURL has_any ("%0A","%0a","%0D","%0d","%0d%0a","\n","\r")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, ReceivedBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kubectl apply of attacker-crafted Rancher import URL (authImage payload delivery) AIDelivery High
Detects a cluster operator fetching or applying the malicious Rancher import manifest — kubectl/oc apply or curl/wget against a URL containing /v3/import/ and the authImage parameter. This is the victim-side delivery step the advisory requires ('victim must execute kubectl apply against a maliciously crafted URL'). Rationale: Anchors on the article's required victim action (kubectl apply of a crafted URL) plus the concrete '/v3/import/' path and 'authImage' parameter, matched in the process command line — near-zero legitimate use of that exact combination. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mhc6-2gfq-xx62 • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2026-44939
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1610
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("%0A","%0a","%0D","%0d") or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"authImage=[^\s&]*(command|hostPath|hostNetwork)"
Response runbook
1) Triage: URL-decode the authImage value in the captured command line; benign onboarding has an OCI image reference, exploitation has embedded newlines + injected YAML keys. Identify the operator account and host. 2) Contain: isolate the host if the manifest was applied, revoke the cluster registration token used in the URL, and rotate the cattle service account and any cluster credentials per the advisory guidance. 3) Hunt: query Kubernetes audit logs for the resulting DaemonSet in cattle-system and check control-plane nodes for containers spawned from the injected command: field.

Rancher /v3/import registration-token enumeration or cross-source reuse AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts abuse of the cluster-import endpoint: a single source IP requesting many distinct registration tokens (enumeration) — the /v3/import/{token}_{clusterId}.yaml format is token-gated and the advisory notes tokens leak via docs/screenshots. Surfaces reconnaissance and leaked-token reuse ahead of the actual injection. Rationale: Derives the token position directly from the article's endpoint format /v3/import/{token}_{clusterId}.yaml and the advisory's note that these tokens leak; counting distinct tokens per source IP is the cleanest enumeration signal available in web logs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mhc6-2gfq-xx62 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-44939
ATT&CKT1190 T1589
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Load balancer or NAT egress IP aggregating many legitimate operators behind one source address
  • CI/CD automation that bulk-registers clusters during a fleet rollout
  • Backup/inventory tooling walking the Rancher API
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("10.0.0.0/8 rancher-mgmt-nat")  // replace with your Rancher management egress IPs after baseline
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the SourceIP's request pattern — is it a known Rancher management node/NAT, or an unfamiliar external IP hitting many tokens in seconds? Check whether any request also carried an authImage newline payload. 2) Contain: if unrecognized, block the SourceIP and invalidate all registration tokens it touched; rotate tokens that may have leaked via docs/screenshots. 3) Hunt: for each token the source successfully retrieved, look for a follow-on kubectl apply on operator endpoints and for new DaemonSets in cattle-system on the corresponding downstream clusters.

Unpatched Argo CD Repo-Server Flaw Could Let Attackers Take Over Kubernetes Clusters

The Hacker News
2026-07-01 11 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Argo CD, a widely used tool for deploying software to Kubernetes, has an unpatched flaw in its repo-server component that lets an unauthenticated attacker run code, provided they can reach the component's internal network port. Synacktiv, which found the bug, says it can lead to a full cluster takeover. There is no fix and no CVE. The firm says it reported the flaw to Argo CD's maintainers in

CVEsCVE-2024-31989 CVE-2025-55190 CVE-2026-42880
ATT&CKT1190 T1204.002 T1219 T1528

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Argo CD repo-server / kustomize spawning shell or network utility (unauth GenerateManifest RCE) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Privileged / host-namespace workload created by Argo CD service account · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Non-Argo-CD process connecting to Argo CD Redis on 6379 (cache-poisoning path, CVE-2024-31989 revival) · [LLM] ClusterRoleBinding granting cluster-admin to an Argo CD service account · [LLM] Argo CD namespace secret enumeration (Redis password / repo credential harvest) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Argo CD repo-server / kustomize spawning shell or network utility (unauth GenerateManifest RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the Synacktiv Argo CD repo-server RCE: an unauthenticated GenerateManifest request sets kustomize's --helm-command to an attacker-supplied script pulled from a hostile Git repo, so kustomize executes that script instead of helm. The high-fidelity signal is the argocd-repo-server / kustomize / helm / git process tree spawning bash, sh, curl, wget, nc or python — none of which appear in a normal git-fetch-then-render workflow. Rationale: Uses the concrete Argo CD process names (argocd-repo-server, kustomize, helm, git) named in the article as parents, paired with shell/network-tool children that never appear in a legitimate git-fetch→kustomize-render path. Cross-checked against Synacktiv's writeup (kustomize --helm-command abuse) and TheHackerNews. Cross-checked against: • https://www.synacktiv.com/en/publications/caught-in-the-octopus-trap-unauthenticated-rce-in-argo-cd-with-codeql • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom Config Management Plugins (CMPs) legitimately configured to shell out (e.g. a plugin wrapping helm via bash)
  • Debug/troubleshooting: an SRE 'kubectl exec'-ing into the repo-server pod and running curl or bash interactively
  • Helm hooks or kustomize plugins that legitimately call python during rendering
  • Init/side-car tooling that fetches over curl during pod startup and shares the same process ancestry
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--config-management-plugin","plugin.yaml") or IsInitiatingProcessRemoteSession == true)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine of the child and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine of kustomize — look for --helm-command pointing at a non-helm path, or curl/wget to an external host, or an interactive shell. Confirm the pod is argocd-repo-server. 2) Contain: cordon the node, kill the repo-server pod, and rotate the Argo CD Redis password and all Git repository credentials the pod could read; enforce the Argo CD NetworkPolicy set (networkPolicy.create=true). 3) Hunt: pivot on the same aid/DeviceName for outbound connections to Redis :6379 and to unknown Git hosts, and review Kubernetes audit logs for Application/pod creations by the argocd service account in the following minutes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("argocd-repo-server","kustomize","helm","git")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","python","python3","perl")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ASCDeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("argocd-repo-server","kustomize","helm","git")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","python","python3","perl")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Argo CD Repo-Server or Kustomize Spawning Shell or Network Tool
id: 6f2a1c9e-4b7d-4a1e-9c2f-8d3e5a7b1c40
status: experimental
description: Detects argocd-repo-server or its kustomize/helm/git subprocesses spawning an interactive shell or network utility, consistent with the unauthenticated GenerateManifest --helm-command RCE disclosed by Synacktiv.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html
  - https://www.synacktiv.com/en/publications/caught-in-the-octopus-trap-unauthenticated-rce-in-argo-cd-with-codeql
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/08
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.execution
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/argocd-repo-server'
      - '/kustomize'
      - '/helm'
      - '/git'
    Image|endswith:
      - '/bash'
      - '/sh'
      - '/dash'
      - '/zsh'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '/nc'
      - '/ncat'
      - '/socat'
      - '/python3'
      - '/perl'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Custom Config Management Plugins that legitimately shell out during manifest generation
level: high
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/(argocd-repo-server|kustomize|helm|git)$/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(bash|sh|dash|zsh|curl|wget|nc|ncat|socat|python3?|perl)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("argocd-repo-server","kustomize","helm","git") AND Processes.process_name IN ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","python","python3","perl")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("argocd-repo-server","kustomize","helm","git") AND Processes.process_name IN ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","python","python3","perl")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Non-Argo-CD process connecting to Argo CD Redis on 6379 (cache-poisoning path, CVE-2024-31989 revival) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the manifest-cache poisoning step: after RCE, the attacker steals the Redis password and writes to the unsigned 'mfst' cache so the next sync deploys attacker workloads. The article notes the cache is still unsigned, so any pod that can reach Redis can poison it. Flags TCP/6379 connections whose initiating process is NOT one of Argo CD's own components or redis-server itself. Rationale: Anchors on the article-specific Redis port 6379 plus Argo CD's own component binary names as the allowlist; CVE-2024-31989 corroboration confirms the unsigned 'mfst' cache and 'any pod can reach Redis' precondition. Any other process on 6379 is the poisoning connection. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9766-5277-j5hr • https://cycode.com/blog/revealing-argo-cd-critical-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1210 T1565.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Prometheus redis_exporter or other metrics scrapers polling 6379
  • An SRE running redis-cli from a bastion/jump pod for legitimate debugging
  • A shared Redis instance reused by another in-cluster app on the same port
  • Service-mesh sidecars (Envoy/Istio) proxying the connection and appearing as the initiating process
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("redis_exporter","redis-cli","prometheus","telegraf","envoy")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process/pod and whether it belongs to Argo CD; capture the command line and source pod IP. If it is redis-cli, a shell, or an unknown binary, treat as suspicious. 2) Contain: rotate the Argo CD Redis password immediately (the cache is unsigned, so a stolen password re-opens the attack), quarantine the source pod, and enable the Argo CD Redis NetworkPolicy so only Argo CD components reach 6379. 3) Hunt: correlate with repo-server shell/curl spawns (UC1) on the same node and review Kubernetes audit logs for Application/pod creations in the sync window that followed.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 6379
| where isnotempty(InitiatingProcessFileName)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("argocd-repo-server","argocd-application-controller","argocd-server","argocd-applicationset-controller","redis-server","redis")
| summarize Count=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by FirstSeen desc
ASCDeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 6379
| where isnotempty(InitiatingProcessFileName)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("argocd-repo-server","argocd-application-controller","argocd-server","argocd-applicationset-controller","redis-server","redis")
| summarize Count=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, AccountName
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: Unexpected Process Connecting to Argo CD Redis Port 6379
id: b1d47a02-3c8e-4f16-9a5b-2e9c7f4d6a11
status: experimental
description: Detects a network connection to TCP 6379 (Argo CD Redis) from a process that is not an Argo CD component or redis-server, consistent with the unsigned manifest-cache poisoning path (CVE-2024-31989 revived).
references:

  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9766-5277-j5hr

Privileged / host-namespace workload created by Argo CD service account AIInstallation High
Hunts the payoff of the takeover: after poisoning the cache, Argo CD deploys an attacker-supplied workload on the next sync. Flags Kubernetes API create/update/patch of pods or controllers performed by an argocd service account whose spec requests privileged, hostPID, hostNetwork, hostIPC, or a docker.sock hostPath — i.e. a container escape / cluster-takeover payload rather than a normal app. Rationale: Uses the article's exact takeover mechanic (Argo CD deploys an attacker workload on next sync) plus the argocd service-account principal and container-escape spec fields (privileged/hostPID/hostNetwork/docker.sock). Argo CD normally deploys unprivileged app workloads, so these host-namespace requests from its SA are high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.synacktiv.com/en/publications/caught-in-the-octopus-trap-unauthenticated-rce-in-argo-cd-with-codeql • https://cycode.com/blog/revealing-argo-cd-critical-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1610 T1611
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate privileged DaemonSets managed via GitOps (CNI plugins, node-exporter, CSI drivers, log shippers) that Argo CD genuinely deploys
  • A platform team intentionally syncing a hostNetwork ingress controller through Argo CD
  • Security agents (Falco, Defender for Cloud sensor) deployed cluster-wide with privileged host access
  • Initial bootstrap sync of a new cluster where many infra components carry host namespaces
Suppression filter
| where not (Namespace in ("kube-system","monitoring","falco") and tostring(ObjectRef.resource) == "daemonsets")
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the RequestObject for the flagged create — confirm the image registry/repoURL is expected and whether privileged/hostPID/docker.sock is justified for that app. Check the git commit and Argo CD Application that drove the sync. 2) Contain: pause auto-sync on the affected Application, delete the malicious workload, and revoke/rotate the argocd service-account token and Redis password; block the source image registry. 3) Hunt: enumerate all recent Applications for external/attacker repoURLs, review UC1/UC2 hits on repo-server, and check for new ClusterRoleBindings granting the argocd SA cluster-admin (UC4).
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Stage == "ResponseComplete"
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where tostring(ObjectRef.resource) in ("pods","deployments","daemonsets","statefulsets","replicasets")
| where Username has "system:serviceaccount:argocd" or Username has_any ("argocd-application-controller","argocd-applicationset-controller")
| where RequestObject has_any ('"privileged":true','"hostPID":true','"hostNetwork":true','"hostIPC":true','docker.sock','/var/run/docker.sock')
| project TimeGenerated, Username, Verb, Namespace=tostring(ObjectRef.namespace), Resource=tostring(ObjectRef.resource), Name=tostring(ObjectRef.name), UserAgent, RequestUri
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:(create OR update OR patch) @objectRef.resource:(pods OR deployments OR daemonsets OR statefulsets OR replicasets) @user.username:system\:serviceaccount\:argocd* (@requestObject.spec.hostPID:true OR @requestObject.spec.hostNetwork:true OR @requestObject.spec.hostIPC:true OR @requestObject.spec.template.spec.hostPID:true OR @requestObject.spec.template.spec.hostNetwork:true OR @requestObject.spec.containers.securityContext.privileged:true OR @requestObject.spec.template.spec.containers.securityContext.privileged:true OR @requestObject.spec.volumes.hostPath.path:*docker.sock*)
CLOUD
index=* sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" stage=ResponseComplete verb IN ("create","update","patch") "objectRef.resource" IN ("pods","deployments","daemonsets","statefulsets","replicasets") "user.username"="system:serviceaccount:argocd*"
| where like(_raw,"%\"privileged\":true%") OR like(_raw,"%\"hostPID\":true%") OR like(_raw,"%\"hostNetwork\":true%") OR like(_raw,"%\"hostIPC\":true%") OR like(_raw,"%docker.sock%")
| table _time user.username verb objectRef.namespace objectRef.resource objectRef.name userAgent sourceIPs{}
| sort - _time
ClusterRoleBinding granting cluster-admin to an Argo CD service account AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts privilege escalation after repo-server compromise: the attacker binds an Argo CD service account (or a new one) to cluster-admin to cement full cluster control. Flags creation of a ClusterRoleBinding/RoleBinding whose roleRef is cluster-admin (or admin) and whose subjects reference an argocd service account. Rationale: Grounded in the article's 'full cluster takeover' claim: cementing control requires elevated RBAC. Anchors on the concrete argocd subject plus cluster-admin roleRef, which is rare outside the initial Argo CD install and therefore high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4192188/argo-cd-flaw-shows-why-gitops-infrastructure-should-be-treated-as-tier-zero.html
ATT&CKT1098 T1548
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Initial Helm/manifest install of Argo CD which creates its application-controller ClusterRoleBinding
  • A platform team legitimately widening Argo CD RBAC to manage a new cluster scope
  • GitOps-managed RBAC where Argo CD itself reconciles ClusterRoleBindings from a trusted repo
  • Cluster bootstrap tooling (Terraform/Cluster API) re-applying the Argo CD RBAC bundle
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "argocd-application-controller" and Username !has "system:serviceaccount:kube-system"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm who created the binding (user.username / UserAgent) and whether it maps to a known GitOps install pipeline versus an interactive or repo-server-originated call. Inspect the subjects and roleRef. 2) Contain: delete the unauthorized ClusterRoleBinding, rotate the referenced service-account token, and review the argocd SA's effective permissions. 3) Hunt: check for privileged workloads created by that SA (UC3), repo-server shell activity (UC1), and Redis connections (UC2) in the same window; audit for any additional new service accounts.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Stage == "ResponseComplete" and Verb == "create"
| where tostring(ObjectRef.resource) in ("clusterrolebindings","rolebindings")
| extend RoleRef = tostring(RequestObject.roleRef.name)
| extend Subjects = tostring(RequestObject.subjects)
| where RoleRef in ("cluster-admin","admin")
| where Subjects has "argocd"
| project TimeGenerated, Username, Verb, Resource=tostring(ObjectRef.resource), BindingName=tostring(ObjectRef.name), RoleRef, Subjects, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Argo CD namespace secret enumeration (Redis password / repo credential harvest) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts credential access via the Argo CD internal surface: the attacker reads the Redis password and Git repository credentials (the recurring pattern the article cites — CVE-2025-55190 leaking repo creds, CVE-2026-42880 exposing plaintext secrets). Flags a single principal performing get/list on many distinct secrets in the argocd namespace within a short window — a secret-harvest fan-out rather than a targeted single read. Rationale: Grounded in the article's explicit theme that Argo CD's internal surfaces keep handing out repo credentials and plaintext secrets (CVE-2025-55190, CVE-2026-42880) plus the Redis-password theft in this attack. The fan-out threshold on the concrete 'secrets' resource in the 'argocd' namespace separates a harvest from routine single reads. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://www.synacktiv.com/en/publications/caught-in-the-octopus-trap-unauthenticated-rce-in-argo-cd-with-codeql
ATT&CKT1552.007 T1552.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Argo CD application-controller / server legitimately listing repo and cluster secrets during reconcile
  • A backup tool (Velero) snapshotting the argocd namespace including secrets
  • An operator running 'kubectl get secrets -n argocd' during troubleshooting
  • Sealed-secrets or external-secrets controllers reconciling many secrets in a burst
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has_any ("argocd-application-controller","argocd-server","velero","external-secrets","sealed-secrets")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the principal (user.username / service account) and UserAgent behind the fan-out; distinguish argocd's own controllers/backup tooling from kubectl, a generic client, or a repo-server-originated call. Note which secrets were read (repo creds, redis). 2) Contain: rotate every secret that was enumerated — Redis password, all Git repository credentials, and cluster secrets — and revoke the token used. 3) Hunt: correlate with repo-server shell/curl activity (UC1) and Redis :6379 connections (UC2) on the same timeline, and watch for subsequent privileged deploys (UC3) or RBAC changes (UC4).
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Stage == "ResponseComplete"
| where Verb in ("get","list","watch")
| where tostring(ObjectRef.resource) == "secrets"
| where tostring(ObjectRef.namespace) == "argocd"
| summarize DistinctSecrets = dcount(tostring(ObjectRef.name)), Secrets = make_set(tostring(ObjectRef.name), 50), Reads = count() by Username, UserAgent, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DistinctSecrets >= 5   // >=5 distinct argocd secrets in 10m = harvest fan-out (repo creds + redis credential); single reads are normal
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:(get OR list OR watch) @objectRef.resource:secrets @objectRef.namespace:argocd
CLOUD
index=* sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" stage=ResponseComplete verb IN ("get","list","watch") "objectRef.resource"="secrets" "objectRef.namespace"="argocd"
| bucket _time span=10m
| stats dc(objectRef.name) as DistinctSecrets values(objectRef.name) as Secrets count as Reads by _time user.username userAgent sourceIPs{}
| where DistinctSecrets >= 5
| sort - _time

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent

                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0c
status: experimental

The Hacker News

Peter Stokes, 19, a dual U.S. and Estonian citizen, appeared in a Chicago federal court on June 30, where a judge ordered him held in custody. Finnish police

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Entra help-desk MFA/password reset followed by sign-in from new IP (Scattered Spider ATO) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] External/guest identity active in Teams during breach response (Scattered Spider watching defenders) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Entra help-desk MFA/password reset followed by sign-in from new IP (Scattered Spider ATO) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts Scattered Spider's signature account-takeover: an IT-help-desk-driven credential or MFA-method reset immediately followed by a successful sign-in for that same user from a different IP within one hour. Article-specific because the body explicitly states the group phones help desks to 'reset a password or approve a login' — this correlates the reset event to the first attacker login. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit claim that Scattered Spider convinces help desks to 'reset a password or approve a login'; correlates the Entra/AD reset event to the first successful sign-in from a different IP within 1h — the actual ATO moment. Cross-checked against CISA AA23-320A which documents help-desk MFA-method reset (T1556.006). Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://www.ic3.gov/CSA/2025/250729.pdf • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1556.006 T1078
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate help-desk password reset when a genuinely-locked-out employee then signs in from home (different IP than the help-desk agent)
  • User travels and legitimately re-registers MFA from a new location after losing a device
  • VPN/proxy egress causes the post-reset sign-in IP to differ from the reset-request IP for the same real user
  • Bulk password-reset campaigns after an org-wide forced credential rotation
  • Self-service password reset from a mobile network (carrier IP) immediately followed by desktop sign-in
Suppression filter
| where DeviceTrustType != "Compliant" and Country != "<user home country>"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the reset event's InitiatedBy — was it a help-desk/admin account or true self-service? Compare ResetIP vs FirstSignInIP geolocation/ASN and check if the sign-in device is compliant/known. Contact the user out-of-band (not via Teams/chat) to confirm they requested the reset. 2) Contain: if unconfirmed, revoke all refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), disable the account, and force a re-registration of MFA under IT supervision. 3) Hunt: review the same account's sign-ins, mailbox-rule creation, OAuth app consents, and Teams/chat joins in the following 24h; check whether the help-desk agent handled other suspicious resets in the same shift.
let win = 1h;
let resets = IdentityDirectoryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Account Password reset","Account Password changed")
| project ResetTime = Timestamp, TargetUpn = AccountUpn, ResetActor = AccountName, ResetDetail = tostring(AdditionalFields)
| where isnotempty(TargetUpn);
resets
| join kind=inner (
    AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ErrorCode == 0
    | project SignInTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Country, City, Application, DeviceTrustType
) on $left.TargetUpn == $right.AccountUpn
| where SignInTime between (ResetTime .. ResetTime + win)
| summarize arg_min(SignInTime, *), FirstSignInIP = any(IPAddress) by TargetUpn, ResetTime
| extend DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', SignInTime, ResetTime)
| project ResetTime, SignInTime, DelayMin, TargetUpn, ResetActor, FirstSignInIP, Country, City, Application, DeviceTrustType
| order by ResetTime desc
let win = 1h;
let resets = AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where LoggedByService in ("Authentication Methods","Core Directory","Self-service Password Management","Account Provisioning")
| where ActivityDisplayName has_any ("Reset user password","Reset password (by admin)","Admin registered security info","User registered security info","Admin updated security info","User started security info registration")
| extend TargetUpn = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName)
| extend InitiatedByUpn = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| extend ResetIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| where isnotempty(TargetUpn)
| project ResetTime = TimeGenerated, ActivityDisplayName, TargetUpn, InitiatedByUpn, ResetIP;
resets
| join kind=inner (
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ResultType == 0
    | project SignInTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, SignInIP = IPAddress, AppDisplayName, Location
) on $left.TargetUpn == $right.UserPrincipalName
| where SignInTime between (ResetTime .. ResetTime + win)
| where SignInIP != ResetIP
| summarize arg_min(SignInTime, *) by TargetUpn, ResetTime
| extend DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', SignInTime, ResetTime)
| project ResetTime, SignInTime, DelayMin, TargetUpn, ActivityDisplayName, InitiatedByUpn, ResetIP, SignInIP, AppDisplayName, Location
| order by ResetTime desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:("Reset user password" OR "Reset password (by admin)" OR "Admin registered security info" OR "User registered security info" OR "Admin updated security info")
External/guest identity active in Teams during breach response (Scattered Spider watching defenders) AIActions on Objectives Low
Hunts the joint-advisory behaviour the article calls out: once inside, Scattered Spider 'lurk in a company's chat tools and join the calls it holds to respond to the breach.' Surfaces guest/external (#EXT#) identities joining Teams meetings, being added to teams/chats, or reading messages — a signal an intruder is monitoring the incident-response effort. Rationale: Directly implements the article's quoted advisory line about intruders joining the breach-response calls/chat; pivots on guest/#EXT# identity performing Teams meeting-join and message-read operations, which is not covered by generic phishing/exec rules. Corroborated by CISA AA23-320A on Scattered Spider persistence in collaboration tooling. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1213.005 T1078.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate external partners/MSSP/DFIR retainer consultants invited into the actual incident-response bridge (expected guests)
  • Vendor or auditor guest accounts routinely joining recurring cross-org meetings
  • Contractors with B2B guest access participating in normal project chats
  • New guest onboarding during M&A or partner integration generating MemberAdded events
  • External Teams federation for legitimate customer-support conversations
Suppression filter
| where UserId !has_any ("@trusted-mssp.com","@dfir-retainer.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each guest identity, verify the invitation provenance — who added them (check the corresponding AuditLogs 'Add member to group'/'Invite external user' event), when the guest tenant/domain was first seen, and whether it aligns with a sanctioned partner. Prioritize guests added AFTER the breach-response channel was created. 2) Contain: if unrecognized, remove the guest from all teams/meetings, block the external domain in Teams federation/guest-access policy, and move IR coordination to an out-of-band channel the attacker cannot see. 3) Hunt: correlate the guest's AccountId/IP with SigninLogs and the reset-correlation detection above; review what channels/files the guest accessed and whether the same external domain appears in OAuth consents or mailbox forwarding.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType in ("MemberAdded","TeamsSessionStarted","MeetingParticipantDetail","MessagesListed","ChatCreated","MessageSent")
| extend RawUpn = tostring(RawEventData.UserId)
| where AccountType == "Guest" or RawUpn has "#EXT#" or AccountDisplayName has "#EXT#"
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, AccountId, AccountType, RawUpn, IPAddress, CountryCode, City, ObjectName
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in ("MemberAdded","TeamsSessionStarted","MeetingParticipantDetail","MeetingDetail","MessagesListed","ChatCreated","MessageSent","MemberRoleChanged")
| where ExternalAccess == true or UserType == "Guest" or UserId has "#EXT#"
| project TimeGenerated, Operation, UserId, UserType, ExternalAccess, ClientIP, UserAgent, ObjectId
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
